subsection: 11. Science, technology and medicine; case study: the invention and early history of the motor car, 1871–1920

notes.b: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who worked in France. Her research on radioactivity made her one of the most important scientists of the period.
points: Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw in 1867, and she studied in Paris, where she married the physicist Pierre Curie in 1895.
Curie began research on radioactivity after Henri Becquerel found that uranium emitted rays in 1896, and she coined the term radioactivity.
In 1898 the Curies announced the discovery of polonium, named after Poland, and of radium, which they isolated in 1902.
Curie shared the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1903 with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, becoming the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
She won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry in 1911 for her discovery of polonium and radium and her isolation of radium, making her the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in different sciences.
During the First World War she developed mobile X-ray units, known as petites Curies, which were used to examine wounded soldiers close to the front.
Curie became the first woman professor at the University of Paris, the Sorbonne, in 1906, after Pierre's death in an accident that year.

Contemporaries admired her work, although some French politicians and scientists were hostile to a woman in a leading scientific post; historians today see her as one of the founders of modern physics and chemistry.
Her long exposure to radiation caused the leukaemia from which she died in 1934, and the danger of radiation was not fully understood during her lifetime.

notes.h: Medicine: germ theory, vaccines and surgery
notes.b: The discovery that microbes cause disease transformed medicine and surgery between 1870 and 1920.
points: Louis Pasteur's experiments in the 1860s and 1870s showed that microbes cause fermentation and disease, which led to the germ theory of disease.
Pasteur developed pasteurisation, the heating of liquids to kill microbes, and he produced vaccines for chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies.
In 1885 Pasteur treated Joseph Meister, a boy bitten by a rabid dog, with a rabies vaccine, and the treatment succeeded.
Robert Koch identified the bacterium that causes tuberculosis on 24 March 1882, and he identified the cholera vibrio in 1883.
Koch's postulates set out the conditions that must be met to prove that a particular microbe causes a particular disease.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery in the late 1860s, using carbolic acid to kill microbes on wounds and instruments, which reduced infection after operations.
Anaesthetics, first used in surgery in the 1840s, including ether and chloroform, allowed longer and more complex operations, and chloroform was used in childbirth in Britain after 1853.
The Nobel Prize for Medicine was awarded to Koch in 1905, recognising his work on tuberculosis.
Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in November 1895 while working at Würzburg, and he received the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901.
X-rays were quickly used in medicine to locate broken bones and bullets, and they were used in field hospitals during the First World War.
Thomas Edison developed the phonograph in 1877 and the practical incandescent light bulb in 1879, which spread electric lighting through cities in the 1880s and 1890s.
Guglielmo Marconi transmitted wireless signals across the Atlantic in December 1901, when he received a signal in Newfoundland from Cornwall, and he shared the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1909.
The telephone, invented in 1876 by Alexander Graham Bell, became a widely used means of communication by the 1900s.
The Wright brothers, Orville and Wilbur, made the first controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903.
Aircraft were used by all the belligerent powers in the First World War for reconnaissance, bombing and fighting in the air, and the development of the aeroplane accelerated during the war.
By 1920 air travel was still limited, but regular airmail services and passenger routes had begun in several European countries.

notes.h: Case study: the invention of the motor car, the engine and early design
notes.b: The motor car emerged in Germany and France in the 1880s and 1890s from the development of the internal combustion engine and the bicycle industry.
points: Nikolaus Otto built a practical four-stroke internal combustion engine in 1876, which became the basis of nearly all petrol engines.
Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach developed a high-speed petrol engine at Cannstatt in the 1880s, and in 1885 they built the Reitwagen, a motorcycle with a wooden frame.
Karl Benz built a three-wheeled petrol-powered vehicle in Mannheim in 1885 and patented his Motorwagen on 29 January 1886, which is generally regarded as the first practical automobile.
Benz's company was founded in 1883 as Benz and Company, and it sold the Motorwagen commercially in the late 1880s.
Bertha Benz made the first long-distance drive by car in August 1888, travelling from Mannheim to Pforzheim, about 106 kilometres, with her sons, to demonstrate the car's practicality.
In France, Panhard et Levassor and Peugeot began building cars using Daimler engines in the 1890s, and Louis Renault built his first car in 1898.
John Boyd Dunlop, a veterinary surgeon in Belfast, patented the pneumatic tyre in 1888, which made cars and bicycles more comfortable and gave a boost to tyre manufacturers.
Michelin, a French tyre firm, developed detachable pneumatic tyres in 1891, which made tyre repair easier for motorists.

notes.h: Case study: the motor car, mass production and the Model T
points: Henry Ford founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903, and in 1908 it launched the Model T, a simple and durable car designed for mass production.
The Model T was sold in large numbers in the USA, and Ford reduced its price steadily through improvements to production, which made the car affordable to ordinary workers.
Ford introduced the moving assembly line at Highland Park, Michigan, in 1913, which cut the time needed to assemble a car from more than twelve hours to about ninety minutes.
In January 1914 Ford announced a daily wage of five dollars for workers at the plant, which was much higher than the wage in most other industries.
Mass production spread the techniques of the assembly line to other industries in Europe and the USA, and Ford's methods were studied closely by European manufacturers.

notes.h: Case study: the motor car, economic and social effects, 1900–1920
points: The car industry stimulated demand for steel, rubber, glass and oil, and it created new jobs in manufacturing, repair and sales.
Road building and the regulation of traffic increased as cars became more common, and motorists began to campaign for better roads and fewer restrictions.
During the First World War motor vehicles were used to carry troops and supplies; the Paris taxis that carried French troops to the Marne in September 1914 became a symbol of this.
Motor transport, motor ambulances and armoured cars were used by the belligerent armies, and military needs encouraged further development of engines and tyres.
The car changed leisure, allowing people to travel for pleasure and encouraging the growth of tourism, while also creating new dangers from road accidents.

Historians differ on the car's wider effect: some see it as a central driver of twentieth-century consumer society, while others argue that its impact before 1920 was more limited to wealthy and urban groups.

notes.h: Assessment: science and technology as drivers of change
notes.b: Science and technology brought major gains in medicine, communications and industry, but their benefits and risks were distributed unequally.
points: Achievement: germ theory and antiseptic surgery reduced death from infection after operations, and vaccines saved many lives from diseases such as rabies.
Limit: knowledge of radiation danger came too late for many early researchers and technicians, including Curie.
Achievement: the motor car and the assembly line transformed transport and production, and by 1920 the car was a central part of industrial economies in the USA and Europe.
Limit: the benefits of the car and the assembly line were concentrated among wealthy and urban groups in the years before 1920, while the rural poor had little access to them.
Contemporaries often saw science as a source of national progress and prestige, while later historians stress the links between scientific research and military and industrial power.

keyTerms.definition: An engine that burns fuel inside a cylinder to drive a piston, which Otto's four-stroke design made practical in 1876.
The spontaneous emission of rays from certain elements such as uranium, radium and polonium, studied by Marie Curie and others from 1896.
The principle that many diseases are caused by microbes, which Pasteur and Koch established through experiment in the 1870s and 1880s.
The use of chemicals, such as carbolic acid, introduced by Joseph Lister to kill microbes on wounds and instruments and reduce infection.
A system of mass production in which each worker performs a single task on a product that moves past them, introduced by Ford at Highland Park in 1913.
A tyre filled with compressed air, patented by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888, which improved the comfort and speed of bicycles and cars.
